why: Simulate the DFS stack against the given order: the next vertex must be an unvisited neighbour of the deepest stack vertex that still has unvisited neighbours, because DFS only backtracks out of a vertex once all its neighbours are visited. Tracking each vertex's count of unvisited neighbours makes the check linear.
hints: In a recursive DFS, when does the search leave a vertex and return to its parent?
Only after every neighbour of that vertex is visited. So before placing order[i], pop stack vertices with no unvisited neighbours; then order[i] must be adjacent to the new top.

Keep rem[v] = number of unvisited neighbours (decrement neighbours on each visit), adjacency sets for O(1) membership, and a stack. Validate length, range, duplicates and order[0] == 0 first. O(n + edges).
pitfalls: You may not pop a vertex that still has unvisited neighbours, even if order[i] is adjacent to an ancestor (example 3).
Check length n, repeats, out-of-range values and that the order starts at 0 before simulating.
Order entries can be any 32-bit integer, so range-check before indexing.
